1035.bp: When you chat with a search assistant across multiple turns, asking follow-up questions and building on earlier responses, how do you actually know if it's doing a good job? This paper tackles the real-world problem of measuring whether conversational search systems work well—a task that's become critical as chatbots handle more complex information-seeking tasks.
1035.wh: The tricky part is that traditional evaluation methods, which compare outputs to reference answers, don't fit well here because conversations are dynamic; each turn depends on the previous one, and what counts as 'good' changes as the conversation unfolds. Meanwhile, using language models as judges is faster and cheaper than hiring humans, but these AI judges often get things wrong in biased ways and don't generalize well across different systems and datasets.
1035.ap: FACE works by breaking down each conversational turn into small, meaningful pieces—the core information units—and scoring each piece according to different criteria (like relevance or clarity). Instead of using a fixed prompt to score everything, it uses a search-then-optimize strategy called beam search and bandit optimization to find the best prompt instructions for each specific aspect of quality. These optimized prompts are then applied consistently to score the atomic pieces, which get rolled up into an overall dialogue score.
1035.ww: This works because it tackles two real problems at once: by scoring small chunks rather than whole conversations, you catch problems at the granular level where they actually occur, and by optimizing prompts for each quality aspect independently, you avoid the bias that comes from a single all-purpose prompt. The optimization approach learns which prompts are actually effective rather than guessing.
1035.po: The result is that FACE correlates far more reliably with human judgments than existing methods, and because the optimized prompts transfer across different language models and datasets, you can reuse the same approach on new systems. Most importantly, it doesn't just give a single number—it breaks down exactly which parts of the conversation failed and where, making it actionable for system builders.

1036.bp: When you ask a search system to write a long, detailed answer to a complex question, you need to pull in facts from many different documents. The real-world challenge here is ensuring your answer covers all the important angles—if you only find facts about symptom management but miss prevention and epidemiology, your answer is incomplete even if what you did find is correct.
1036.wh: Dense retrieval systems (which find documents by comparing meaning rather than keywords) are built to find relevant documents, but 'relevant' usually means one-to-one: does this document answer this query? They don't naturally optimize for bringing back diverse angles or comprehensive coverage. If you want multiple different perspectives on a question, you get back similar documents that cover the same ground, and the system never explores the edges of the topic.
1036.ap: CoveR trains a neural retrieval system using two learning objectives that work together: one based on picking documents that cover different aspects of the question (built from synthetic training data where each document is labeled for which sub-question it answers), and one based on copying learned knowledge from simpler systems. The training data itself comes from breaking down long questions into natural sub-questions and using language models to judge whether candidate documents would answer each sub-piece.
1036.ww: This works because by teaching the system to explicitly model which sub-questions each document addresses, you force it to learn what diversity actually means for this task. The twin learning objectives—one pushing for breadth across angles and one preserving the ability to find truly relevant items—create a natural tension that produces a system optimizing the trade-off rather than collapsing to either extreme.
1036.po: CoveR retrieves 10% more novel, non-redundant facts than baseline methods while maintaining the same ability to find relevant documents. This matters directly for long-form generation: an AI writing a comprehensive answer gets both the relevant pieces and the missing angles, producing answers that feel complete rather than lopsided.

1037.bp: A keyphrase is a concise phrase capturing what a document is really about—the words you'd use to index it in a library or tag it in a search engine. Extracting these automatically is important because it gives you a quick summary of each document's essence, which flows into recommendation, search, and content organization systems.
1037.wh: Modern language models are great at finding keyphrases that are semantically important across the whole document, but documents aren't uniform: they have multiple sections, and a phrase might be important only for understanding one subtopic buried on page three. A global importance score misses these local, subtopic-specific keyphrases that matter if someone is reading that particular section.
1037.ap: MUDY uses two different scoring channels in parallel: one that estimates how likely a language model would naturally generate each candidate phrase (a measure of semantic centrality), weighted by how unique that phrase is in its local context; and another that inspects the internal attention patterns of the language model at different scales—both across the whole document and within individual segments—to measure how much focus the model pays to each candidate.
1037.ww: By examining the model's internal attention at multiple scales, you're essentially asking: 'At what levels does this model consider this phrase important?' A phrase might be ignored globally but highlighted within its section, and that local signal matters. The dual approach captures both the semantic weight of a phrase and its contextual salience—different concepts measured in parallel.
1037.po: MUDY extracts more keyphrases correctly across multiple real datasets, especially at picking out the subtle, locally-important phrases that traditional methods miss. The method also reveals something deeper: by checking what keyphrases the model should have found but didn't, you learn what your extraction system actually does and doesn't understand about the document.

1038.bp: Dense retrieval systems like ColBERT compress whole documents down to dense numerical vectors that let you quickly find relevant results. The problem is they do this per-token—every single word gets its own vector stored in memory—so searching through millions of documents means storing billions of vectors, which is expensive and slow.
1038.wh: Existing attempts to throw away low-importance token vectors either pick them randomly or use heuristic scores like 'does this token appear often in the data?' These approaches don't have a principled justification—they work sometimes, but you don't really know when or why, and you often lose important tokens by accident.
1038.ap: This paper thinks about tokens geometrically: it treats each token's embedding as occupying a region in high-dimensional space (called a Voronoi cell in mathematics), and argues that a token is important if its region is large—meaning it covers a lot of ground that wouldn't be covered if you removed it. By computing these regions using heat-diffusion kernels, the authors derive a principled score for each token's actual contribution to the system's ability to distinguish documents.
1038.ww: The insight is that importance isn't a property of the token in isolation; it's about whether the token occupies unique territory in embedding space or whether other nearby tokens would capture the same information anyway. If you prune a token whose region is completely covered by its neighbors, nothing breaks. But if you prune a token that uniquely occupies a region, you lose discrimination power.
1038.po: This geometric framework lets you prune away 20-30% of tokens without hurting retrieval quality, shrinking your index substantially. More importantly, because the approach is grounded in geometric principles rather than heuristics, it's more predictable and interpretable—you can look at which tokens got pruned and understand why the system thought they were redundant.

1039.bp: Long conversations with a chatbot—where you ask a question, get an answer, ask a follow-up, refine, build on that, and keep going—naturally accumulate a lot of history. The challenge is: how do you remember everything useful without your context window exploding, while still being able to retrieve and weave together memories from earlier in the conversation when they're relevant to a new question?
1039.wh: Simply summarizing old conversations loses the thread—you squash rich details into a paragraph and lose the narrative structure that made each exchange meaningful. Cramming everything in memory works until your context limit, then you're stuck choosing what to forget. And when you do need to retrieve a memory to answer a new question, you have to search through a flat list of summaries rather than a structured mental map.
1039.ap: Dynamic Memory Forest (DMF) organizes conversation history like a forest of trees: each conversation session gets 'consolidated' into thematic units that preserve the logical flow of that session, then these units are arranged into tree structures and dynamically connected to existing trees through a voting mechanism that decides whether a new session 'attaches' to previous related sessions or stands alone. Retrieval uses entropy—measuring uncertainty—to decide which memory trees might hold relevant answers to the current question.
1039.ww: This mimics how human memory actually works: related memories cluster together, and you navigate by following associations rather than searching a database. By preserving the internal structure of each session (consolidation) while allowing sessions to link dynamically (growth), the system keeps both detail and navigability. The entropy-driven search means you explore uncertain regions where the answer might hide.
1039.po: A system using DMF can maintain coherent conversations over many sessions without forgetting important details or losing track of conversational threads. When you ask a new question, the system can find and recall relevant earlier moments even if they're separated by many turns, because they're organized by theme rather than chronology.

1040.bp: Evaluating search systems requires human judges to label whether retrieved results actually answer the search request. But this labeling is expensive and slow, and it's becoming common to use language models as judges instead. The question this paper asks is: does it actually work better if you give the LLM judge a detailed, structured description of what the user is looking for, rather than just the search query?
1040.wh: When judges (human or AI) only see a bare query like 'machine learning', they interpret it wildly differently—one person thinks you want algorithms, another thinks you want applications, another thinks you want theory. This high disagreement makes it hard to tell if retrieval systems are actually getting better or if you're just getting lucky with your judge.
1040.ap: The researchers take language models and use them to write out structured topic descriptions that include context, background, and specific boundaries—essentially formalizing what the user was really asking for. They compare LLM judges working from bare queries against LLM judges working from these richer descriptions, testing on real search benchmarks with hundreds of documents labeled by humans.
1040.ww: When the judge sees the full context of the information need, it can make more consistent, defensible decisions about relevance. Bare queries are ambiguous; a structured topic is less so. The result is that agreement improves—both between different LLM judges and between LLM judges and humans—because everyone is interpreting the same underlying request.
1040.po: LLM judges working from structured topics are substantially more reliable than those working from queries alone. This simple finding has a direct payoff: if you want to evaluate search systems cheaply using LLMs, you should invest the effort to formalize your information needs rather than just copying over the original query.

1041.bp: Cross-domain recommendation means: you've built a great recommendation system for movies, but now you want to use that knowledge to recommend books. You have rich data on what users liked in movies (the source domain) and you want to transfer that understanding to make better book recommendations (the target domain), especially when you have little book data.
1041.wh: The standard approach trains the system separately in each domain, learns a mathematical function to transform the movie-understanding into book-understanding, then applies that transformation. The problem is you're throwing away information: when you transform from one domain to another, you lose the specific details about what the user actually did in each domain. A user who loves action movies but rarely buys books is different from a user who loves action movies and buys books constantly—that source-and-target history together tells you something special.
1041.ap: SetCDR directly uses each user's full history—their movie ratings and their book ratings together—as a set of item-rating pairs. Instead of processing these sequentially (which would require defining an arbitrary order), it uses a neural architecture that doesn't care about order: the network produces the same result whether you feed in the history chronologically or shuffled. A lightweight label attaches to each history item, marking whether it came from movies or books.
1041.ww: Order-invariance is powerful here because user history is fundamentally unordered: it's a collection of things they did, not a sequence. Traditional neural networks are built for sequences and either force an arbitrary order or require special tricks to ignore it. By using an architecture that naturally handles sets, you remove noise and get cleaner signals. The domain label lets the model learn different patterns from different domains without one overwhelming the other.
1041.po: SetCDR makes better recommendations in the target domain, especially when target-domain data is scarce. Because it processes both histories directly without losing information to transformation, it captures the nuance of cross-domain transfer: how a user's source-domain preferences actually inform what they'll like in the target domain.

1042.bp: Recommendation systems are increasingly using language models to understand items and users, then generating an ID or index token representing the item to recommend. The problem is that the same user's history might be described differently depending on how you write the prompt, or which item attributes you choose to emphasize, and this variation creates inconsistency.
1042.wh: If you ask a language model to recommend the next book for a reader using a detailed prompt, you get one answer. Use a simpler prompt emphasizing different aspects, and you get a different answer. Neither is wrong, but they disagree. Averaging or picking one doesn't work well because the recommendations are often based on genuinely different understanding of what the user wants—they're not just noise, they're different valid perspectives.
1042.ap: MVIGER learns to treat prompt variations and different item-indexing schemes as different information sources, each with their own lens on the user's preferences. It models which source to trust or whether to blend multiple sources as a learnable decision: during training it learns what combination of perspectives tends to be right, and at test time it can either pick the single best source or adaptively blend them based on the situation.
1042.ww: Instead of fighting the variation, this approach embraces it: each prompt or indexing scheme does capture something real about the user's interests, just from different angles. By learning to weight or combine these perspectives intelligently, you get robustness—the system doesn't break if the prompt changes, because it learned that variation is normal and meaningful.
1042.po: MVIGER gives consistent, high-quality recommendations regardless of how you've written your prompts or chosen your indexing scheme. Users get better recommendations, and system builders can iterate on prompts without worrying about accuracy degradation.

1043.bp: Imagine searching for a specific scene in a massive library of untrimmed video—say, finding the moment in a cooking video where they add salt. You need to both find the right video and pinpoint the exact moment within it. This is video corpus moment retrieval, and it matters for video search, content moderation, and video summarization.
1043.wh: Standard retrieval systems compare shallow visual and textual features—like color histograms or keyword overlap—which can't capture semantic subtlety. A query about 'adding salt' is visually and texturally very different from salt-adding scenes in the video: you're looking for salt-related visual concepts and keywords, but the real signal is semantic understanding.
1043.ap: Video-GAR flips the problem: instead of trying to match query to video, it trains the system to reconstruct the query from video segments. This reconstruction ability becomes a signal that the system deeply understands what's in the video. It uses an efficient backbone (Bi-Mamba) that processes video efficiently, a fusion module with a decoder that helps the system calibrate its understanding without slowing down inference, and a localization strategy that explicitly models where moments begin and end.
1043.ww: Reconstructing the query from the video segment requires genuine semantic understanding, not just surface-level matching. If the system can reliably generate the original query from a video moment, it must have captured the semantic essence. The efficient backbone keeps computational costs down, while the training-only decoder provides supervision without runtime overhead.
1043.po: Video-GAR retrieves relevant moments more accurately and localizes them more precisely than discriminative baselines, across standard benchmarks. Because it's built on reconstruction and semantic understanding rather than pattern matching, it handles fine-grained queries better.

1044.bp: Recommending the next place to visit based on where someone has been is the core of location-based recommendation systems. But people's actual locations are complicated: sometimes you go to a café because you love it, sometimes because it's the only place near your office and you have to grab lunch somewhere.
1044.wh: Standard systems assume every check-in directly reveals what you truly like, but real human behavior is mixed: some visits are authentic choices, others are external constraints. Worse, people sometimes go to a place that's close to where they actually wanted to go but was too far or unavailable. If the system treats all these equally, it learns a distorted preference map that doesn't match what users genuinely want.
1044.ap: MPDC attacks this from two angles: it uses a behavior-aware component that looks at contextual patterns (like the difference between morning commute and evening browsing) to separate authentic preference signals from context-driven behavior, and a spatial-aware component that infers where users probably wanted to go based on their overall movement patterns and the distances they typically travel. The system uses diffusion-based contrasting learning, which learns by asking: which alternatives would a truly preferred location look like?
1044.ww: By modeling the gap between observed behavior and true preference, you correct for the bias in raw data. The spatial awareness captures the idea that small deviations from a location often indicate the true target wasn't available or wasn't obvious. Diffusion-based learning helps the system explore what valid alternatives look like, building a more accurate mental map.
1044.po: MPDC recommends locations more accurately, especially for users with complex mobility patterns. By filtering out context-driven noise and recovering intended destinations, it learns what users actually prefer rather than what their forced behavior suggests.

1045.bp: Recommendation systems often discover that users have multiple distinct interests: someone might like both action movies and documentaries, but not as an average of the two—they're genuinely different moods. Multi-interest recommendation tries to capture this by generating multiple user 'profiles' each representing a different facet.
1045.wh: The problem is that weighted averaging methods (the standard approach) end up blending all interests together into a smooth average, losing the distinctness that makes each interest useful. You wanted to distinguish 'action fan' and 'documentary fan' but instead get 'action-documentary blend', which doesn't reflect how the user actually behaves.
1045.ap: DMI uses diffusion models—probabilistic systems that add noise then learn to remove it—to extract interests. Rather than reconstructing a single next item (which tempts the model to collapse everything into a middle-ground prediction), it reconstructs the full multi-interest vectors themselves. A cross-transformer module looks at specific subsets of the user's history relevant to each interest, guiding the diffusion to extract interest-specific patterns rather than merging them.
1045.ww: By reconstructing the full interest space rather than downstream items, you preserve the independence of different interests. The model can't cheat by merging them into an average because there's no single item to optimize for—it must preserve the structure. The history-guided diffusion ensures that each extracted interest actually has support in what the user did.
1045.po: DMI produces more distinct, non-overlapping multi-interest representations, leading to better recommendations when the system actually has multiple interests. By preventing over-smoothing, it captures the real diversity in user behavior.

1046.bp: Session-based recommendation operates on limited data: a user arrives with no prior history and performs a few actions in one session (clicking items, maybe buying), then you must recommend next items. You can't build a rich user profile the way you do with years of history.
1046.wh: Language models are powerful at understanding behavior, but they're expensive and sometimes hallucinate—they confidently claim preferences that don't match the actual session data. In session-based settings where context is already scarce, hallucinations are especially damaging. Also, using an LLM for every user at inference time is computationally infeasible for large platforms.
1046.ap: SPRINT uses LLMs selectively: during training, only on sessions where the model is uncertain about intent, and it validates predicted intents by checking whether they actually improve recommendations. The LLM outputs are constrained to choose from a global pool of common intents, reducing hallucination. At inference, a lightweight neural intent predictor learned during training handles all sessions without calling an LLM.
1046.ww: By using LLMs only for difficult cases during training, you get their semantic reasoning power where you need it most without paying the inference cost. Validating against recommendation performance filters out hallucinations: if the LLM's intent doesn't improve recommendations, it's discarded. The lightweight predictor at inference captures what the LLM learned without the computational burden.
1046.po: SPRINT outperforms state-of-the-art methods and scales to real-world session-based systems because it captures LLM reasoning during training but runs efficiently at inference. Recommendations are also more interpretable because they're tied to discovered session intents rather than opaque user embeddings.

1047.bp: Recommendation systems store a dense numerical vector for every user and item, which lets them quickly compute similarity and make recommendations. At scale, storing billions of vectors consumes enormous memory. Hashing is a standard trick: map many vectors to the same bucket, saving space.
1047.wh: Hashing forces crude choices: if two vectors hash to the same bucket, they're treated as identical even if they're different. This hurts both accuracy (you lose meaningful distinctions) and personalization (users with different preferences get mapped to the same representation).
1047.ap: Graph Diffusion Gated Embeddings (GDE) uses a different approach: instead of hashing, it precomputes heat-diffusion patterns from a small set of 'seed' vectors, using mathematical kernels that diffuse influence from each seed across the graph. These diffusions become probabilistic gates that mix a small set of learnable embeddings. Each node (user or item) gets represented by a weighted combination of seed embeddings determined by its diffusion pattern.
1047.ww: Diffusion naturally explores the local structure around each seed, so similar nodes get similar diffusion patterns and thus similar mixing weights. By using probabilistic mixing instead of hard bucket assignments, you preserve nuance: two slightly different nodes still get meaningfully different representations even if they rely on overlapping seed embeddings.
1047.po: GDE achieves better accuracy on both retrieval and click-through rate prediction than hashing methods, using a much smaller embedding table. Because the mixing is soft and structure-aware, the system is both more accurate and more personalized.

1048.bp: Active learning on graphs means: you have a partially labeled network of nodes (like papers with some labeled topics, some not) and you want to intelligently choose which unlabeled nodes to label next to improve your classifier most efficiently. In practice, you'll encounter novel node types you didn't know existed when you started labeling.
1048.wh: Existing active learning algorithms assume all classes are known upfront and just find informative nodes for known classes. But real-world graphs are open-world: new categories emerge after you start. You need an algorithm that both improves classification on known classes and discovers entirely new ones, but existing methods don't handle both.
1048.ap: The approach uses hierarchical clustering: first cluster nodes in feature space to find promising regions of the graph (rather than looking at individual nodes), then within the selected cluster, use semi-supervised sub-clustering to find the single most informative example. It scores cluster informativeness not just by classification uncertainty but by measuring whether the cluster likely contains novel classes. A self-distillation loss helps the network learn to produce clustered embeddings.
1048.ww: By working at the cluster level first, you can efficiently explore large unlabeled regions and spot where novelty is likely hiding (clusters with mixed properties are prime candidates for novel classes). Once you've identified a promising region, fine-grained sub-clustering picks the best single example to label. The dual objective prevents the system from ignoring either known-class improvements or novel-class discovery.
1048.po: The algorithm discovers new classes while improving classification on known classes, more efficiently than methods that focus only on known-class uncertainty. By identifying informative regions rather than just informative points, it explores the graph's structure effectively.

1049.bp: Short video platforms need to recommend what to watch next by understanding user preferences from their behavior. But 'behavior' on short video platforms is nuanced: a like, a follow, a share, and a watch-till-end all mean different things about what the user wants.
1049.wh: Binary models (like/dislike) lose this nuance, treating all engagement the same. Temporal models that ignore action type miss that the sequence of action types is meaningful—first you watch, then you like, then you follow conveys something different from the reverse sequence.
1049.ap: A2Gen models the specific actions users took (like, follow, watch-till-end, etc.) as a sequence over time, using an attention module to enrich each action with contextual information from the video it was applied to. A hierarchical encoder learns temporal patterns in the action sequences. Finally, the system generates the next action sequence that it expects, and uses that prediction to recommend items.
1049.ww: By modeling actions as a sequence, you capture that user intent evolves over time and through interaction: watching suggests interest, then liking confirms satisfaction, then following commits to future recommendations. The generation approach learns not just what items to recommend but what engagement pattern will follow—which is a richer signal of preference.
1049.po: A2Gen makes recommendations for short video that account for user engagement sophistication, improving accuracy by capturing the patterns in how users interact (not just what items they engage with). The action-sequence model is also interpretable: you can see what engagement pattern the system predicted.
